title: Architecture
cardHint: any part of the drawing to read about it

blocks.heading: Four planes
body: Four planes: an always-on **serving plane** at ~$0, a **CI/CD plane** on GitHub Actions, an **ephemeral Kubernetes plane** that exists ~30 minutes a month, and a **monitoring plane** that closes the loop back into training.

A visitor's drawing becomes a prediction, a log line, and — if they grade it — labeled training data. Every merge retrains, gates, and redeploys the model without a human. Every week the logs are scored for drift.

blocks.heading: Serving
body: An always-on serving plane at ~$0. AWS Lambda wakes from zero, runs FastAPI with an ONNX model, and sends the guess back to the canvas.

blocks.kicker: The wire · From Serving to Monitoring
blocks.heading: Logs, every prediction
body: Every prediction Lambda serves is written to S3 as a log line. Every Monday the drift report reads that week's logs and compares them with the training data.

blocks.heading: Evidence & drift
body: Every claim on the site is backed by a published artifact. The evidence hub renders from the MLflow registry. The weekly drift report scores real predictions against a reference distribution; feedback becomes a proxy-accuracy signal; a drift breach opens a GitHub issue.
The site styles all of it — including this very page — from JSON contracts, never from the platform's own HTML.

blocks.kicker: The wire · From Monitoring to CI/CD
blocks.heading: Drift breach → retrain
body: When drift crosses its threshold, the report opens a GitHub issue. A retrain folds the labeled drawings into the training split, and the gate decides whether the result ships.

blocks.heading: The quality gate
body: **Ship and re-crown are decoupled.** Every training run produces a challenger; the gate compares it to the reigning champion on held-out test accuracy, with two rules — an absolute floor (0.85) and no regression beyond a small epsilon. Pass, and the challenger ships.
The champion alias only moves on a strict improvement, so "champion" always means the best-ever bar. A crippled 0.50 model is blocked in CI, deploy steps skip, and the live model is untouched.

blocks.kicker: The wire · From CI/CD to Ephemeral K8s
blocks.heading: The same image
body: The image that serves on Lambda is the one Helm deploys to EKS, by digest — so the monthly load test measures the real thing, not a copy.

blocks.heading: Ephemeral Kubernetes
body: The same serving image that runs on Lambda also runs on Kubernetes — but only for ~30 minutes a month. A workflow does **apply → exercise → destroy**: Terraform brings up EKS and a VPC, Helm deploys the API by image digest, Prometheus scrapes it, k6 drives load, and everything is torn down.
A monthly failsafe sweeps any survivor tagged `tier=ephemeral`, so a botched teardown can't quietly bill. No always-on cluster cost, anywhere.

blocks.kicker: The wire · From CI/CD back to Serving
blocks.heading: A new model ships
body: A challenger that clears the gate is built into an image and deployed to Lambda. This is the wire that closes the loop: canvas → CI → deploy → drift → feedback → retrain.
What stays running when nothing is happening: two storage buckets, one container registry, one function. Everything else is summoned on demand and torn down.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: The home-page canvas. A drawing is sent to the serving API as raw QuickDraw strokes — the `[[xs],[ys]]` coordinates — not as pixels; a yes / no verdict (with a class picker on a no) comes back as a feedback event.

items.heading: Why strokes
items.body: The server owns every transform down to the 28×28 tensor, in the same module the training pipeline imports. Sending raw strokes means the frontend can change without touching how the model sees a drawing — and there is no train/serve skew to drift into.

items.heading: Privacy
items.body: The prediction log stores an input hash, never pixels. A drawing is kept only on an explicit graded verdict, behind an upfront consent notice — no identity, no tracking.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: A FastAPI app running the model as ONNX, reached through a Lambda Function URL. The arm64 container image runs unmodified on Lambda, under `docker run`, and on EKS — no code fork between tiers.

items.heading: Why this choice
items.body: It scales to zero — nothing runs, and nothing is billed, until someone draws. The cold start is honest, and it's the story the home page tells.

items.heading: Trade-offs
items.body: The first request after an idle spell is slow; a warm container would be faster but would cost money doing nothing. The warm-up ping and the cold-start message cover the gap.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: Three buckets. A logs bucket holds predictions, feedback, and labeled captures; a data bucket is the DVC remote, the MLflow store, and the monitoring outputs; a tfstate bucket holds Terraform state. The app writes logs per request, fail-open — an S3 outage costs a log line, never a prediction.

items.heading: Why this shape
items.body: One partitioned store means one lifecycle policy and one place to reason about cost and access. The Lambda execution role can only append to `predictions/`, `feedback/`, and `captures/` — no read, no delete.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: Every Monday, Evidently scores the model's output distribution — predicted-class mix, top-1 confidence, top1−top2 margin — over a 30-day window of real predictions against a reference distribution. It publishes `drift.json` as a data contract.

items.heading: The key call
items.body: It does not alert on the ever-present out-of-distribution drift: real doodles are OOD against QuickDraw's bitmaps by definition, so that fires every week and means nothing. It pages only when the model is doing badly — a confidence collapse or a proxy-accuracy breach. The OOD drift is still measured and published, just not paged on.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: The public hub that backs every claim on this site. It renders from the MLflow registry — the record of which model is champion and what it scored — not from a checked-in snapshot, so it can't show a number that's no longer live.

items.heading: The contract
items.body: Every public-facing output ships as JSON — `evidence.json`, `drift.json`, `feedback.json`, the history files — and the portfolio styles it. The platform's own HTML and Grafana PNGs are demoted to functional artifacts; the look belongs to the site.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: The alert channel. When the drift report sees mean confidence below 0.55, or proxy accuracy below 0.5 with at least ten graded verdicts, it opens — or comments on — a single `drift-alert` issue. It's idempotent: one issue per breach, not one per run.

items.heading: Why an issue
items.body: It puts the signal where the work happens. A breach is a prompt to retrain, and the retrain folds the labeled drawings back into the training split — closing the loop without a dashboard anyone has to remember to check.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: The DVC DAG that runs on every merge touching model inputs: download → preprocess → validate → train (a PyTorch CNN, logged to MLflow) → evaluate → export ONNX → reference. Each stage hashes its code and params, so only what changed re-runs.

items.heading: Validation is a gate
items.body: Training depends on the validation report — a declared Pandera schema over the pulled data. No report, no training; bad data fails the pipeline loudly and early instead of quietly producing a worse model.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: Every run registers a model version and logs its metrics; `champion` and `challenger` aliases track the best-ever bar and the latest candidate. The tracking database is SQLite, synced to S3, so the history reads the same on any machine.

items.heading: Why it's the source of truth
items.body: The evidence hub renders from this registry rather than a committed file, and the champion alias — not a 'currently deployed' flag — is what the gate compares against. The built image digest is what's actually live.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: A CI step that compares the freshly-trained challenger against the reigning champion on held-out test accuracy, with two rules: an absolute floor of 0.85, and no regression beyond a small epsilon (0.005). Pass, and the challenger ships.

items.heading: Ship and re-crown are decoupled
items.body: Passing means 'ship this'; the champion alias moves only on a strict improvement, so 'champion' always means the best-ever bar rather than a record of what's live. A crippled 0.50 model is blocked in CI, the deploy steps skip, and the live model is untouched.

items.heading: Trade-offs
items.body: A too-tight threshold blocks statistically-equal models; it's tuned to a tolerance band rather than a hard line.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: A challenger that clears the gate is built into an arm64 image, pushed to ECR, and the serving Lambda is updated by image digest — not a mutable tag, which can't sneak a different build in. A smoke test then asserts the live model's sha256 matches the ONNX that was just built.

items.heading: Why this choice
items.body: The same image serves the live Lambda and the monthly EKS rehearsal — one artifact, two homes, no drift between them.

items.heading: Trade-offs
items.body: Container cold starts are heavier than a plain zip; acceptable given scale-to-zero and the warm-up ping.

items.heading: What happened
items.body: A challenger regressed against the champion. The gate failed the job, the deploy steps were skipped, and the live model was left untouched.

items.heading: Why it matters
items.body: This is the gate working. The dead-end on the diagram is a real CI run you can open and read for yourself.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: Once a month, Terraform brings up a VPC (two AZs, a single NAT) and an EKS 1.33 cluster with three t4g.small Graviton nodes — for the length of one run, then destroyed unconditionally.

items.heading: Three teardown layers
items.body: A leaked cluster plus NAT costs ~$8–10 a day, so teardown is defended three ways: an `if: always()` destroy that runs on success, failure, or cancel; a scheduled failsafe a few hours later; and the same failsafe as a manual break-glass. The failsafe sweep only touches resources tagged `tier=ephemeral`, pinned by a test.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: Helm deploys the exact serving image Lambda runs, pinned by digest so a mutable tag can't substitute a different build. It's a ClusterIP service with no public load balancer; Prometheus scrapes its `/metrics`.

items.heading: Why by digest
items.body: The monthly load test is only worth running if it measures the real thing. Deploying by digest guarantees the cluster is exercising the same bytes that serve live traffic, not a copy.

items.heading: What it is
items.body: k6 drives 20 virtual users for three minutes against the in-cluster API. kube-prometheus-stack (Prometheus + Grafana) captures `api-metrics.json` and a dashboard image, and everything is uploaded as evidence before the cluster is torn down — so nothing is lost when it goes away.

items.heading: Why ephemeral
items.body: The cluster exists only to prove the model under load. Keeping it alive would burn money for no traffic; capturing the evidence first means the proof outlives the cluster.
